question: Can the mismatch introduced by straight-through gradient estimation in low-precision neural networks be represented as a perturbation of a nearly Euclidean Riemannian metric, decayed through Ricci flow, and converted into a practical, stable quantization-aware training algorithm?

key_findings.claim: The paper reframes STE gradient mismatch as a metric perturbation and proposes RF-DNN, which combines a layerwise natural-gradient-style preconditioner with a finite-difference regularizer inspired by Ricci flow.
key_findings.evidence: The unknown continuous-weight gradient is first written as the copied quantized gradient plus a supposedly small perturbation. The copied gradient is then premultiplied by the inverse of an LNE metric. In practice, RF-DNN uses a weak inverse approximation and adds a loss term intended to make metrics computed from translated inputs satisfy a discrete Ricci-flow equation.

key_findings.claim: The central information-geometric derivation is internally inconsistent: the Hessian of the stated separable convex potential is diagonal, not the dense outer-product metric claimed in Theorem 10.
key_findings.evidence: Equation 13 defines Phi(xi) as a sum over coordinates of log(cosh(tau xi_i))/tau squared. Its Hessian has entries sech-squared(tau xi_i) on the diagonal and zero off diagonal. Equations 14-15 instead assert I minus tanh(tau xi) tanh(tau xi) transposed, which has generally nonzero off-diagonal entries. Appendix E repeats the same step by differentiating a vector expression as though the coordinatewise sum produced an outer product. Consequently the displayed LNE metric, its divergence interpretation, and the natural-gradient claim do not follow from the proposed Bregman potential.

key_findings.claim: Even if the asserted metric is accepted, it is Riemannian only under an unverified high-dimensional norm condition, and the weak inverse approximation can be far from the exact inverse.
key_findings.evidence: Writing v=tanh(tau w), the proposed metric is I-vv-transpose. Its eigenvalues are one in directions orthogonal to v and 1-minus-norm(v)-squared along v, so positive definiteness requires norm(v)-squared below one, not merely bounded individual weights. Its exact Sherman-Morrison inverse is I plus vv-transpose divided by 1-minus-norm(v)-squared; Equation 25 drops that denominator. The paper says tau can make the matrix diagonally dominant but reports no layer-dimension-aware bound or experimental tau value, although a layer can contain many weights.

key_findings.claim: The Ricci-DeTurck stability results do not establish convergence for the neural-network metric actually used by RF-DNN.
key_findings.evidence: The cited geometric results require a complete, one-ended, linearly stable, integrable Ricci-flat manifold and a sufficiently small L2 or L-infinity perturbation. The paper declares the neural parameter metric to be a special Ricci-flat LNE metric from its algebraic form, but does not calculate its curvature, prove completeness or positive definiteness, verify the ALE end conditions, or establish integrability and linear stability for a network. It then replaces the global parameter metric with independent layerwise metrics without proving that the product construction retains those assumptions.

key_findings.claim: The quantity called Ricci curvature in the algorithm is a heuristic based on image translations, not a justified discretization of the Ricci tensor on the weight manifold.
key_findings.evidence: Equation 26 omits the general Christoffel-product terms and is used without a stated normal-coordinate restriction. The authors then set an inverse-metric factor to the identity, discard two derivative terms for experimental fairness, and identify parameter-coordinate derivatives with row and column translations of input images. Four translated forward/backward passes are combined in Equation 28. No map proves that these input transformations are coordinate directions on the parameter manifold or that this finite difference is consistent with Ricci curvature.

key_findings.claim: Driving the discrete-flow residual toward zero neither proves continuous-flow existence nor directly measures or removes STE gradient error, and Algorithm 2 leaves a time-indexing circularity unresolved.
key_findings.evidence: The regularizer in Equation 31 contains g(t+1), yet Algorithm 2 computes it before the loss and before the update that would define the next weights. The text states that constraining this residual ensures existence of the discrete Ricci flow and simultaneous perturbation convergence, but a penalized finite-difference identity does not import the continuous Ricci-DeTurck theorem. The algorithm never observes a ground-truth gradient through the quantizer, so it cannot verify that the modified direction is closer to that nonexistent-or-zero derivative.

key_findings.claim: Under the weak approximation used in every experiment, the distinctive gradient operation reduces to a rank-one, layer-global preconditioner whose benefit is not isolated from the Ricci-inspired regularizer and extra translated passes.
key_findings.evidence: Equation 25 transforms a layer gradient q into q plus v times the inner product of v and q. This is a rank-one correction determined by current weights. The experiments never compare standard STE, LNE preconditioning alone, the translation regularizer alone, their combination, matched extra augmentation, or a generic rank-one preconditioner. Thus accuracy gains cannot be causally attributed to Ricci flow rather than ordinary preconditioning or regularization.

key_findings.claim: The backward algorithm modifies weight gradients but does not clearly address the non-differentiability of quantized activations despite presenting RF-DNN as a weight-and-activation method.
key_findings.evidence: The forward loop quantizes both weights and activations. In the backward loop, however, the metric correction is applied only to the weight gradient, while the activation step uses the ordinary derivative of f and propagates through the discretized weight without an explicit derivative or estimator for Q(a). Several headline experiments also use 1-bit weights with 32-bit activations. The scope is therefore narrower and less specified than the paper's general DNN framing suggests.

key_findings.claim: In matched scratch-training tables, RF-DNN reports modest but consistent classification gains over selected older STE variants.
key_findings.evidence: Across five runs, 1-bit-weight CIFAR-10 accuracy improves over the best listed competitor by 0.89, 0.52, and 0.92 points on ResNet20/32/44. CIFAR-100 gains are 1.85 points for ResNet56 and 0.46 for ResNet110. On ImageNet ResNet18, RF-DNN reports 60.83 top-1 versus 59.83 for FCGrad and 58.34 for DoReFa. The test remains 8.93 points below the cited full-precision ResNet18.

key_findings.claim: The empirical evidence does not validate the proposed mechanism or the claimed exponential convergence of metric perturbations.
key_findings.evidence: No experiment measures the STE gradient angle or error, metric eigenvalues, diagonal dominance, Ricci curvature accuracy, residual N, distance to an LNE metric, or an exponential decay rate. Stability is inferred from the standard deviation of final accuracy and visually noisy test curves. Lower run-to-run accuracy variance can arise from many sources and is not evidence that a geometric perturbation decays under Ricci flow.

key_findings.claim: The state-of-the-art comparison is not a controlled benchmark and mixes external results, bit settings, architectures, and pretraining regimes.
key_findings.evidence: Table 4 compares RF-DNN numbers with values copied from papers from 2018-2021. It spans weight-only and weight-plus-activation settings, different backbones, and separately reported full-precision baselines. It gives no matched implementation, training budget, seed interval, throughput, or hardware result. The 8-bit gains over full precision are only 0.01-0.15 points and cannot be interpreted without uncertainty.

key_findings.claim: The method is not reproducible from the paper and its practical cost is understated.
key_findings.evidence: The experimental section does not report tau, alpha, the four exact translations, how g(t+1) is computed, strong-approximation architecture, initialization of any metric state, or a public implementation. The complexity discussion counts four translation-dependent metric calculations only asymptotically and provides no wall-clock or memory measurements. A dense metric would be quadratic in the number of layer parameters, while exploiting the rank-one form would be linear; neither implementation is specified.

method.core_idea: Treat STE's copied gradient as a natural gradient under a constructed near-Euclidean metric, use Ricci-DeTurck stability theory to motivate suppressing deviations from that metric, and train a quantized network with a weak inverse-metric preconditioner plus a finite-difference flow residual computed from translated inputs.
method.mechanism: A separable log-cosh potential is claimed to induce g=I-vv-transpose with v=tanh(tau w). Backpropagation is redefined layerwise as g-inverse times the quantized-weight gradient. Although a learned dense inverse is proposed, experiments use g-inverse approximately equal to I+vv-transpose. The paper interprets image row and column translations as coordinate variations, computes four corresponding metrics, forms a finite-difference quantity called Ricci curvature, and adds the squared residual of a one-step metric-flow equation to the task loss with coefficient alpha. Continuous weights are updated; discretized weights and activations are used in the forward pass.
assumptions: The difference between the unknown continuous-weight gradient and the STE gradient is a small linear perturbation, even though the quantized objective is discontinuous and its classical derivative is zero almost everywhere.
A gradient discrepancy can be uniquely or usefully represented as a perturbation of a Riemannian metric rather than one of many possible preconditioners.
The stated log-cosh Bregman potential yields the dense metric in Equation 15 despite its coordinate-separable form.
Tau is small enough in every high-dimensional layer to keep I-vv-transpose positive definite and strictly diagonally dominant.
Dropping all higher Sherman-Morrison terms produces an accurate inverse metric during training.
The neural parameter metric is complete, Ricci-flat, one-ended, integrable, and linearly stable, with a sufficiently small L2 perturbation.
Replacing one global metric with layerwise metrics preserves the hypotheses of the Ricci-DeTurck stability result.
Input-image translations define coordinate derivatives on the weight manifold and the resulting finite differences consistently estimate Ricci curvature.
Penalizing a discrete residual containing g(t+1) ensures existence and convergence of a corresponding flow.
The weak layer-global rank-one correction is a better surrogate gradient rather than merely another weight-dependent learning-rate transformation.
Run-to-run accuracy standard deviation is an adequate proxy for gradient stability and metric perturbation decay.
Results from older papers with heterogeneous training and precision settings support a state-of-the-art comparison.

techniques.role: Reinterprets a surrogate-gradient discrepancy as a perturbation of a Riemannian metric.
Uses a log-cosh potential and tanh-transformed weights to define the proposed LNE geometry.
Premultiplies each layer gradient by I plus a rank-one outer product in the weak approximation.
Proposes, but does not experimentally use, an MLP that maps metric entries to an approximate dense inverse.
Invokes Ricci-DeTurck flow to obtain short-time existence and all-time convergence for suitable geometric perturbations.
Uses four small image translations to approximate selected second derivatives of the metric.
Adds a squared finite-difference metric-evolution residual to the task loss.
Constructs an independent metric for each weight layer so it can be inserted into ordinary backpropagation.
Runs discrete weights and activations in the forward pass while retaining continuous latent weights for updates.

evaluations.setting: CIFAR-10 scratch training with 1-bit weights on ResNet20, ResNet32, and ResNet44; five runs
evaluations.metric: Mean and standard deviation of test accuracy sampled from the last ten epochs
evaluations.result: RF-DNN reports 89.83 plus/minus 0.23, 90.75 plus/minus 0.19, and 91.63 plus/minus 0.11.
evaluations.baseline: DoReFa reports 88.28/90.23/90.71 and MultiFCG 88.94/89.63/90.54; cited full-precision results are 91.50/92.13/93.56.

evaluations.setting: CIFAR-100 scratch training with 1-bit weights on ResNet56 and ResNet110; five runs
evaluations.metric: Mean and standard deviation of test accuracy sampled from the last ten epochs
evaluations.baseline: The best listed alternatives are DoReFa at 66.71 for ResNet56 and FCGrad at 68.74 for ResNet110; cited full precision is 71.22 and 72.54.

evaluations.setting: ImageNet scratch training with 1-bit weights and ResNet18; five runs
evaluations.metric: Top-1 and top-5 accuracy over the last five epochs
evaluations.result: RF-DNN reports 60.83 plus/minus 0.41 top-1 and 83.54 plus/minus 0.18 top-5.
evaluations.baseline: DoReFa 58.34/81.47, MultiFCG 59.47/82.41, FCGrad 59.83/82.67, and cited full precision 69.76/89.08.

evaluations.metric: Accuracy mean and standard deviation at 1, 2, 4, and 8 weight bits
evaluations.result: The plotted RF-DNN mean rises with bit width and the authors describe variance as consistently small.
evaluations.baseline: No plain STE, LNE-only, flow-penalty-only, or matched extra-augmentation ablation is shown.

evaluations.setting: CIFAR-100 training and test curves for ResNet56/110
evaluations.result: RF-DNN test accuracy is reported 1.85 points above DoReFa for ResNet56 and 1.05 points above it for ResNet110.
evaluations.baseline: DoReFa only; the figure does not report gradient mismatch, metric residual, perturbation norm, or exponential convergence.

evaluations.setting: ImageNet comparisons across AlexNet, ResNet18, ResNet50, and MobileNet with 1-8 bit weights and 4-32 bit activations
evaluations.metric: Top-1/top-5 accuracy and gap to cited full-precision baselines
evaluations.result: RF-DNN reports 56.39 for 6-bit AlexNet, 67.05 for 1-bit-weight ResNet18, 66.75 for 4-bit ResNet18, 76.07 for 8-bit ResNet50, and 61.32/70.76 for 5/8-bit MobileNet.
evaluations.baseline: Externally reported DeepShift, MD, ELQ, ADMM, QN, MetaQuant, RQ, INT8, and SR+DR results under non-unified protocols.

limitations: The Hessian of the proposed separable convex potential does not equal the metric used by the theory and algorithm.
Positive definiteness, diagonal dominance, and inverse-approximation error are not established for real layer dimensions or measured during training.
The neural metric is asserted rather than proven to satisfy completeness, Ricci flatness, integrability, linear stability, and small-perturbation assumptions.
The layerwise metric substitution is not connected back to the global manifold theorem.
Input translations are not justified as coordinates on parameter space, and the finite-difference expression omits parts of general Ricci curvature.
The regularizer uses a future metric before the parameter update that defines it and lacks an implementable time-order specification.
The method never observes a true gradient through quantization and therefore does not demonstrate that gradient mismatch is reduced.
Activation quantization is present in the forward algorithm but lacks a clear metric-corrected surrogate in the backward algorithm.
No ablation separates rank-one preconditioning, translation augmentation, and the discrete-flow penalty.
No direct mechanism metric is reported: gradient angle, metric eigenvalues, residual norm, perturbation norm, or decay rate.
Tau, alpha, exact translations, metric-state handling, and several implementation details are absent; no code link is provided in the article.
Computational claims omit wall-clock and memory costs of repeated transformed passes and possible dense metric operations.
Scratch baselines are limited to methods from 2016 and 2019, while the broader table copies heterogeneous results from prior papers.
The statistical protocol ambiguously mixes five runs with multiple late-epoch test measurements and gives no confidence tests.
The work evaluates only image classification CNNs; it does not test transformers, language models, detection, segmentation, robustness, or hardware deployment.
The theoretical LNE construction, weak/strong inverse approximations, and much of the convergence narrative already appeared in the authors' 2021 arXiv paper.
failure_modes: For a wide layer, norm(tanh(tau w)) exceeds one and the proposed metric becomes singular or indefinite, invalidating natural-gradient and Ricci arguments.
The missing Sherman-Morrison denominator becomes large near the positivity boundary, so the weak update points or scales very differently from the claimed inverse-metric direction.
A layer-global inner product couples unrelated parameters and lets a few large weights dominate every gradient correction.
The flow penalty learns invariance to selected translations while being misinterpreted as suppression of quantization gradient error.
A provisional next-step metric is detached, stale, or differentiated through inconsistently because Algorithm 2 does not define its computation order.
The four translated passes multiply training time and memory traffic enough to erase the claimed deployment-side efficiency benefit.
Quantized activations still receive a mismatched or implicit STE gradient even if the weight correction helps.
Lower accuracy variance across seeds masks oscillating discrete weights or unstable internal gradients.
Tau small enough to preserve positive definiteness makes v nearly zero and reduces RF-DNN to ordinary STE.
Tau large enough to produce a meaningful correction violates the small-perturbation and inverse-approximation conditions.
Old or mismatched baselines make a small accuracy gain look method-specific when a modern QAT optimizer or quantizer would remove it.
External-table gains disappear under a controlled common full-precision initialization and training budget.
open_questions: What is the correct Bregman potential, if any, whose Hessian equals I minus tanh(tau w)tanh(tau w)-transpose and remains positive definite in high dimension?
Can a layerwise tau schedule guarantee a uniformly bounded condition number without shrinking the correction to zero?
Does the exact Sherman-Morrison inverse outperform the weak approximation at comparable cost?
Can the discrete quantity in Equation 28 be derived consistently from a metric on parameter space rather than assigned through input transformations?
How should g(t+1) be computed without circularity, and is the loss differentiated through that provisional update?
Does RF-DNN reduce a measurable finite-difference or stochastic gradient-bias target compared with STE?
Which component produces the gain: rank-one preconditioning, translated examples, the residual penalty, or their interaction?
Do metric eigenvalues, the flow residual, and perturbation norms exhibit the claimed exponential decay in actual training?
Can the framework explicitly handle activation-gradient mismatch and joint weight-activation quantization?
How does RF-DNN compare under one implementation with ReSTE, ASkewSGD, BiPer, PEGE, transition-rate scheduling, and plain STE tuned equally well?
Are custom metric gradient estimators equivalent to retuned STE under the reparameterization result of Schoenbauer et al.?
Does any benefit survive on modern transformers and low-bit language-model training after accounting for added compute?
reusable_insights: For any proposed natural-gradient quantization method, symbolically differentiate the potential and numerically audit metric eigenvalues before accepting the geometry.
Use the Sherman-Morrison identity for rank-one metric updates; it exposes both the exact low-cost inverse and the singularity condition.
Separate a theorem's manifold assumptions from an analogy to neural parameter space and verify each assumption explicitly.
A finite-difference residual deserves a geometric name only after coordinate consistency and discretization error are established.
Validate surrogate gradients with operational quantities such as directional agreement, discrete loss improvement, transition rate, and training oscillation, not final accuracy alone.
Ablate preconditioning, augmentation, regularization, and quantizer changes in a factorial design so a geometric story is not credited for a generic effect.
Measure metric conditioning throughout training; a tunable parameter that trades effect size against positive definiteness is a central experimental variable.
Report exact computation order whenever a training loss depends on next-step parameters or optimizer state.
Use matched modern baselines and common full-precision checkpoints for QAT; cross-paper accuracy tables are not causal evidence.
Include wall-clock, peak memory, and energy alongside asymptotic notation when extra forward/backward passes are required.
Treat run-to-run output variance and within-run gradient stability as different quantities.
Audit self-predecessors and text overlap when a paper's theoretical core appeared before its application-specific extension.

competitive_landscape.title: Thoughts on the Consistency between Ricci Flow and Neural Network Behavior
competitive_landscape.relationship: direct self-predecessor with substantial theoretical overlap
competitive_landscape.difference: The same author group already presented LNE metrics, Ricci-DeTurck stability, the same log-cosh divergence, the same weak inverse I plus tanh outer product, and the learned strong inverse before RF-DNN. The 2024 JMLR paper's distinct addition is the quantization-gradient framing, input-translation finite differences, the residual loss, and DNN experiments. ArXiv also flags text overlap, so the broad geometric construction is not new to this paper.

competitive_landscape.title: ASkewSGD: An Annealed Interval-Constrained Optimisation Method to Train Quantized Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: ASkewSGD formulates QNN training as a sequence of smoothed interval-constrained problems, gives a first-order method with comparable numerical complexity, and proves convergence under stated objective assumptions. It attacks the discrete optimization problem directly rather than importing continuous Ricci-flow stability, making it a necessary controlled baseline for RF-DNN's claimed theoretical and practical advantages.

competitive_landscape.title: Estimator Meets Equilibrium Perspective: A Rectified Straight Through Estimator for Binary Neural Networks Training
competitive_landscape.difference: ReSTE explicitly measures estimator error and gradient-magnitude variance, shows their tradeoff, and uses a tunable power estimator to balance them on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet. RF-DNN offers a broader geometry narrative but measures neither gradient mismatch nor gradient instability. ReSTE therefore supplies the direct mechanism tests missing from RF-DNN and reports a simpler estimator without auxiliary losses.

competitive_landscape.title: BiPer: Binary Neural Networks using a Periodic Function
competitive_landscape.difference: BiPer replaces sign with a periodic square wave in the forward pass and a matched sine surrogate in the backward pass, derives a frequency-dependent quantization-error analysis, and evaluates modern binary-network baselines on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet. It directly addresses forward/backward inconsistency with a falsifiable quantization parameter and stronger current baselines, while RF-DNN retains sign quantization and adds a weight-space preconditioner plus regularizer.

competitive_landscape.title: Custom Gradient Estimators are Straight-Through Estimators in Disguise
competitive_landscape.difference: Schoenbauer et al. prove that a broad class of nonzero weight-gradient estimators is approximately equivalent to STE under reinitialized weights and rescaled learning rates for sufficiently small-step SGD, and often directly equivalent under adaptive optimizers. Because RF-DNN's experimental update is a weight-dependent custom preconditioner, this work demands tests against retuned STE and an analysis of whether the rank-one correction escapes the equivalence class. RF-DNN reports neither.

competitive_landscape.title: Scheduling Weight Transitions for Quantization-Aware Training
competitive_landscape.difference: This ICCV 2025 work identifies discrete-level transition rate, not latent-weight learning rate, as the operational step-size variable in QAT and uses a transition-adaptive learning rate to schedule it. It measures the actual changes of quantized weights, works with SGD, Adam, and AdamW, and adds about scalar control rather than four translated metric passes. It is a more direct and testable stability mechanism than RF-DNN's unmeasured Ricci residual.

competitive_landscape.title: Progressive Element-wise Gradient Estimation for Neural Network Quantization
competitive_landscape.difference: PEGE progressively mixes full-precision and quantized parameters and corrects the surrogate gradient using elementwise discretization error. With shared forward quantizers, it reports improvements over STE and EWGS on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet, including 4-bit ResNet18 slightly above its full-precision reference. It operationalizes quantization error and directly ablates its schedulers; RF-DNN's corresponding perturbation is latent and never measured.

competitive_landscape.title: Mirror Descent View for Neural Network Quantization
competitive_landscape.difference: Ajanthan et al. derive valid mirror maps from explicit conditions on quantization projections, show the relationship between mirror descent and STE, and provide a stable implementation evaluated across CIFAR, TinyImageNet, and ImageNet. RF-DNN cites this work but does not verify comparable projection or metric conditions; its claimed Bregman metric is algebraically inconsistent. Mirror descent is therefore both a precursor and a cleaner alternative explanation.

competitive_landscape.title: Distance-Aware Quantization
competitive_landscape.difference: DAQ frames quantization as distance-based assignment, uses kernel soft argmax to reduce gradient mismatch, and controls the soft-to-hard quantizer gap with an adaptive temperature. It addresses both mismatch and deployment discrepancy in one explicit quantizer and was absent from RF-DNN's experiments, despite being a direct prior baseline for the central problem.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The paper claims a new geometric account of STE gradient mismatch as metric perturbation, an LNE manifold whose perturbations decay exponentially under Ricci flow, and a practical RF-DNN that improves the accuracy and stability of discretized networks at ordinary training complexity.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The work is ambitious and integrates information geometry, geometric-flow stability, a low-rank gradient correction, and quantization experiments in a distinctive narrative. The scratch tables show consistent gains over the selected DoReFa, MultiFCG, and FCGrad baselines. However, the theory-to-algorithm chain breaks at several points: the stated potential does not yield the claimed metric; the metric may not be positive definite; Ricci-flat and stability assumptions are unverified; image translations are not parameter-manifold coordinates; and a penalized discrete residual does not prove continuous-flow convergence. Experimentally, the paper never measures gradient mismatch or perturbation decay, omits decisive component ablations and key hyperparameters, and relies on old or cross-paper baselines. Much of the LNE/Ricci/weak-inverse construction also appeared in arXiv:2111.08410. Later ReSTE, BiPer, transition-rate scheduling, PEGE, and gradient-estimator-equivalence work make the untested mechanism and benchmark gap more consequential.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The defensible contribution is a Ricci-inspired rank-one preconditioning and translation-consistency recipe for quantized CNN training, accompanied by modest empirical gains—not a demonstrated Ricci-flow solution to gradient mismatch. A useful replication should first correct the metric derivation or discard the Bregman claim; guarantee and log metric conditioning; define the next-step residual causally; and run a factorial comparison of exact versus weak inverse, preconditioner, translations, penalty, and retuned STE. It should measure discrete transition rates, estimator error proxies, residual decay, runtime, and memory against ASkewSGD, ReSTE, BiPer, PEGE, and transition-rate scheduling on current QAT benchmarks.

reviewer_notes: Complete primary pass: all 44 extracted pages were read end to end, including the JMLR article, all definitions and algorithms, the complete Ricci/DeTurck and information-geometry appendices, every table, and the full bibliography. Rendered pages 2, 8, 13, 18, 21, 23, 26-29, and 32 were inspected at original detail to verify the conceptual diagrams, inverse approximation, translation-based curvature construction, algorithm ordering, accuracy tables, stability curves, comparison table, and notation. The separable-potential Hessian and rank-one eigenvalue/inverse claims were independently checked algebraically. Current direct competition was checked through primary arXiv, PMLR, CVF, and OpenReview/proceedings routes as of 2026-08-23, including the 2021 self-predecessor, Mirror Descent, DAQ, ASkewSGD, ReSTE, BiPer, custom-estimator equivalence, transition-rate scheduling, and PEGE. The extracted source is arXiv:2302.03390 updated 2024-12-19 and journal-referenced as JMLR 25(386), published November 2024.
